title: The AI that took their jobs is now renting their faces, for $15

content_html:
In China, the AI boom that put actors and models out of work has found a new use for them. It is renting their faces.

A growing set of platforms now pays people $15 to $700 to license their likeness for AI-generated content, Rest of World reported. Producers browse catalogues of faces by gender, age and category, from “girl-next-door” to “supermodel,” then filter them by genre.

The demand comes from China’s microdrama industry, the ultrashort vertical series made for phones. China released 128,000 of them in the first quarter of 2026. More than 95% used AI in production.

How renting a face works

ActID, a Shenzhen platform launched in March, has registered around 800 users. About 300 agreed to license their image. Two AI productions have licensed roughly ten faces so far, at 99 to 500 yuan ($15 to $74) an episode, with ActID taking a tenth.

Its pitch is unsentimental. “Producers want attractive faces for lead roles, but they also need distinctive ones like elderly people,” said the company’s marketing chief, Camille Yan. AI dramas “don’t require acting ability anyway; the faces serve as source materials.”

New Claw, a Chengdu platform, pivoted into the business after AI wrecked its old one as a production house. It sets a floor of 500 yuan ($74) per image so users do not undercut each other.

“Traditional drama production declined, advertising budgets shrank,” said its operations lead, Long Lyu. Even luxury brands, he added, are shifting to AI. Selling the rights to a photo at least gives people a way to earn.

The problem the platforms cannot fix

The platforms present themselves as a fix for the theft already happening. Ordinary people keep finding their faces in AI dramas they never agreed to appear in.

Two influencers accused ByteDance’s Hongguo of lifting their faces for a drama that drew more than 40 million views. The platform pulled it. ByteDance says it has removed over 85,000 videos with unauthorised AI reproductions of faces and voices since early 2026.

The courts are filling with such cases. The Guangzhou Internet Court has heard around 700 over three years. In March, a Beijing court ruled that an unauthorised AI face-swap breaks the law even after editing the image.

A legal marketplace is meant to route around all that. Yile Deng, a Beijing lawyer who handles these cases, called it a step toward proper frameworks. Then she named the catch.

Once a face enters an AI marketplace, its owner effectively loses long-term control of it, she said. Platforms cannot stop unauthorised face-swapping, illegal data collection or future model training on the images. “The licensing terms are often so vague that it’s impossible to know who will ultimately use the likeness, or for what purpose.”

The people who know best are refusing

Xu Fang, a 21-year-old model in Shanghai, is suing a fashion brand over a face he says it used on products he never modelled. Even with the platforms paying, he will not sell the rights to his own face.

“If I license my face, I have no idea how AI might eventually change it or whether it could portray me in degrading ways,” he said.

Chinese law already requires consent before biometric data is processed, and bars fabricating a likeness without permission, Digital Trends noted. Enforcement is the hard part. The same pattern of non-consensual AI imagery plays out on other platforms, from Grok images to footage filmed on smart glasses.

There is a final irony. The marketplace may not even take hold, because the economics that created it also limit it. Most AI minidramas still use fully synthetic faces, one director told Rest of World, since buying a real one is optional. “At the end of the day, cost control is what matters most.”

It is the same calculation that keeps China’s AI industry ahead of the rules meant to govern it. A face is now a line item: priced, licensed and, once uploaded, no longer entirely its owner’s.

content_html_zh:
在中国，人工智能的蓬勃发展让演员和模特失业，但它们却找到了新的用途。 这是在租他们的脸。

据《世界其他地区》报道，越来越多的平台现在向人们支付 15 至 700 美元，以获得人工智能生成内容的肖像权。 制片人按性别、年龄和类别（从“邻家女孩”到“超模”）浏览面孔目录，然后按类型进行过滤。

这种需求来自中国的微剧行业，即为手机制作的超短垂直剧。 2026年第一季度，中国释放了12.8万个。 超过 95% 在生产中使用了人工智能。

租用一张脸的运作方式

深圳平台 ActID 于 3 月推出，已注册用户约 800 名。 大约 300 人同意授权他们的形象。 到目前为止，两部 AI 作品已经获得了大约 10 个面孔的授权，每集价格为 99 至 500 元（15 至 74 美元），其中 ActID 占据了十分之一。

它的音调是不带感情色彩的。 “制片人希望主角有有吸引力的面孔，但他们也需要像老年人这样独特的面孔，”该公司营销主管卡米尔·严(Camille Yan)说。 AI剧“反正不需要演技，脸就是素材”。

成都平台 New Claw 在 AI 摧毁了其旧有的制作公司后，转向了这一业务。 它设定每张图片 500 元（74 美元）的底价，这样用户就不会互相压价。

“传统戏剧制作下降，广告预算缩减，”其运营负责人吕龙表示。 他补充说，即使是奢侈品牌也在转向人工智能。 出售照片的版权至少为人们提供了一种赚钱的方式。

平台无法解决的问题

这些平台将自己定位为针对已经发生的盗窃行为的解决方案。 普通人不断在他们从未同意出现的人工智能戏剧中找到自己的面孔。

两位有影响力的人指责字节跳动的洪国为了一部观看次数超过 4000 万的电视剧而抬脸。 平台拉了它。 字节跳动表示，自 2026 年初以来，它已删除了超过 85,000 个未经授权的人工智能复制人脸和声音的视频。

法庭上充斥着这样的案件。 广州互联网法院三年来已审理约700起案件。 今年三月，北京一家法院裁定，未经授权的人工智能换脸行为即使在编辑图像后也违法。

合法的市场旨在解决所有这些问题。 处理这些案件的北京律师邓一乐称，这是迈向适当框架的一步。 然后她给这条渔获命名。

她说，一旦一张脸进入人工智能市场，它的所有者实际上就失去了对其的长期控制。 平台无法阻止未经授权的换脸、非法数据收集或未来对图像的模型训练。 “许可条款通常非常模糊，以至于不可能知道谁最终会使用这些肖像，或者出于什么目的。”

最了解的人却拒绝

上海 21 岁的模特徐芳正在起诉一家时尚品牌，因为他称该品牌在他从未做过模特的产品上使用了该品牌的脸。 即使平台出钱，他也不会以自己的面子出售版权。

“如果我许可我的脸，我不知道人工智能最终会如何改变它，也不知道它是否会以有辱人格的方式描绘我，”他说。

Digital Trends 指出，中国法律已经要求在处理生物识别数据之前必须征得同意，并且禁止未经许可伪造肖像。 执行是最困难的部分。 同样的非共识人工智能图像模式也出现在其他平台上，从 Grok 图像到智能眼镜上拍摄的片段。

最后还有一个讽刺。 市场甚至可能无法站稳脚跟，因为创造它的经济学也限制了它。 一位导演告诉《世界其他地区》，大多数人工智能迷你剧仍然使用完全合成的面孔，因为购买真实的面孔是可选的。 “归根结底，成本控制才是最重要的。”

正是基于同样的计算，中国的人工智能产业始终领先于监管规则。 一张脸现在是一个订单项：定价、获得许可，并且一旦上传，就不再完全属于其所有者。
